{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"When a scheduling system changes your shift with a few hours’ notice, the software appears to be moving boxes on a screen. It’s doing something more serious. It’s deciding whether you can arrange childcare, catch a bus, attend a class, or sleep at a human hour. The timetable looks neutral because the machine doesn’t display the life that has to bend around it. Your time is treated as empty space, available for somebody else to fill.

That is why unpredictability is a form of control. A fixed shift lets you plan, and planning lets you make commitments outside the workplace. You can share care with another person, book an appointment, join a union meeting, or take a second job. When the schedule changes suddenly, those choices become expensive gambles. We should call the result what it is: control exercised through uncertainty.

The usual sales language says the system is “flexible.” There’s a useful distinction here. Flexibility for the worker means having room to respond to changing circumstances. Flexibility imposed by management means the worker must remain ready for changes made elsewhere. One is an ability you can use; the other is a demand that your life stay unfinished. The software isn’t merely recording availability. It’s manufacturing obedience from the fear of being marked unreliable.

Ask what the algorithm knows and what it leaves out. It may know the number of people required at a particular hour. It may know which workers have accepted previous changes. It may know that a shift was offered and declined. It doesn’t know the rent that arrives on Friday, the child who needs collecting, or the bus route that stops running after midnight. It can count a refusal, but it can’t count the cost of compliance. Our employers receive a neat data point; you receive the mess.

This is where the language of choice becomes bullshit. A worker can technically refuse a shift, yet the refusal may affect future hours, a performance score, or a supervisor’s opinion. I think a choice surrounded by penalties is a threat wearing a name tag. It’s formally voluntary and materially coercive. The screen presents two buttons, but your circumstances have already narrowed the corridor between them.

The harm spreads beyond the individual shift. If you expect the schedule to move, you learn to keep every evening provisional. You delay friendships, medical care, education, and collective action. You may stop agreeing to things because you can’t trust that you’ll be free to attend. That is the quiet victory of unpredictable scheduling: it breaks the bridges between workers before anyone has to break a union. The system doesn’t need to ban solidarity when it can make solidarity difficult to schedule.

We can answer this with rules that put time back into the hands of the people who perform the work. A schedule should arrive far enough in advance to be usable, and a late change should carry a premium rather than a punishment. Workers should have a real right to decline, with no reduction in future hours and no hidden score attached to the decision. The system’s records should be visible, contestable, and subject to collective bargaining. You’re entitled to know what the software records about your availability and how those records affect your pay.

I want organisers to treat scheduling data as workplace evidence, not as an oracle. Collect the original schedule, every alteration, the notice given, and the resulting loss or expense. Compare the promises made by the vendor with the decisions the system produces. We can show that a supposedly efficient tool transfers risk downward, one altered shift at a time. I mean the demand quite literally: predictable time is part of compensation, because a wage cannot restore hours that an employer has made unusable. I don’t think the answer requires perfect software. It requires a boundary: our lives are not spare capacity in somebody else’s machine.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o12: named authorities, linked reporting, quoted language, or earlier arguments tested","why":"The request supplies no verified source, quotation, named opponent position, or linked reporting to introduce."}],"refused":""}
